blocks.text:
Design a web search engine, the system that takes a short text query typed by a user and, in a few hundred milliseconds, returns a ranked list of the most relevant pages out of a corpus of tens of billions of crawled web pages. This problem picks up exactly where this category's web crawler design left off, that system solved discovering and fetching pages politely and at scale, and this one solves the very different problem of actually finding and ranking the right handful of pages out of everything that has been crawled, for an arbitrary query, fast enough for a human to wait for it interactively.

The technique that makes this possible at all is an inverted index, a structure that maps each individual word to the list of documents containing it, turning "find documents containing this word" from a scan of the entire corpus into a single, direct lookup.

blocks.text: A user should be able to submit a free-text query and receive a ranked list of matching pages, each with a title, URL, and a short snippet. Results should be ranked by genuine relevance, not merely by whether a query word appears somewhere on the page. The index should be rebuilt from newly crawled or updated pages on a regular, ongoing basis. The system should keep returning results even when some portion of the index is temporarily unavailable or slow.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and satisfying every one of them at once is what makes this a genuinely hard system to design.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and satisfying every one of them at once is what makes this a genuinely hard system to design.

blocks.alt: Low latency, a scalable index, relevance quality, reasonable freshness, and graceful degradation

blocks.text: Low latency means a result has to come back in a few hundred milliseconds, no matter how large the underlying corpus has grown to. Scalability means the index itself is far too large to live on one machine and has to be split across many. Relevance quality means keyword matching alone is not enough, a page that happens to contain a query word but says nothing useful about it should not outrank a genuinely authoritative source, and the ranking itself has to resist being gamed by spam. Freshness here means new and updated pages should show up in search results within a reasonable window, not the instant they are crawled. And graceful degradation means one slow or failed piece of the index should cost a query a little completeness, never fail it outright.

blocks.text: This design assumes crawling itself is already solved, by this category's web crawler problem, and starts from a continuously arriving stream of crawled pages as its input. Ranking blends two signals, term-frequency-based relevance and an offline-computed, link-based authority score per page, rather than any personalization. Index freshness is eventually consistent, a page's update becomes searchable on the next index snapshot publish, not instantly. A slow or failed index shard is excluded from a given query rather than blocking it, covered further in section 20.

blocks.text: A real web search engine's corpus runs into the tens of billions of indexed pages. At real scale, query volume can reach tens of thousands of queries per second at peak, each one needing to complete within a latency budget of a few hundred milliseconds. Neither an inverted index for tens of billions of documents nor the computation needed to score them against an arbitrary query fits on a single machine, which is exactly why the index is split across thousands of shards, each one small enough to stay fast, with every query fanned out across all of them in parallel.

blocks.text: A query enters through a load balancer to a query coordinator, which tokenizes it and scatters it out to every index shard in parallel. Each shard scores its own slice of the corpus locally and returns its own top candidates, which a merger combines, blends with offline-computed link authority scores, and ranks into a single final result list, caching the outcome for popular queries. Separately, the offline side of the system consumes newly crawled pages, tokenizes them, and builds them into the index shards that the query side reads from.

blocks.alt: A query is tokenized and scattered to document-partitioned index shards; their local top results are merged, blended with offline link authority scores, cached, and returned, while an offline pipeline builds the index from crawled pages

blocks.text: Rather than scanning every document's full text for every query, an inverted index precomputes, for every distinct term in the corpus, the exact list of documents that contain it, along with how many times it appears in each. A query then becomes a handful of direct lookups into this structure, one per query term, instead of a scan of the entire corpus.

blocks.alt: A document's text is broken into terms, each term maps to a posting list of document ids and term frequency, and a query term becomes a direct lookup rather than a full document scan

blocks.text: A single query is sent to every shard at once, and the coordinator waits for each shard's local top results up to a fixed timeout. A shard that responds in time is included in the final merge; one that is too slow or has failed is simply excluded, and the query still completes using whichever shards did respond.

blocks.alt: A query fans out to every shard in parallel; shards that respond in time are included in the merge, while a too-slow or failed shard is excluded without blocking the rest of the query

blocks.text: A document's final ranking score blends two genuinely different signals. Term frequency measures how strongly a document matches the query itself, how often the query's words actually appear in it. Link authority, computed offline from the web's link graph, measures how important other pages consider this page to be, independent of any specific query. Neither signal alone is enough, a document can match a query's words perfectly while being low-quality or spam, and a highly authoritative page is useless for a query it has nothing to do with, so the final score blends both together.

blocks.text: The externally visible surface here is deliberately small, one query endpoint, since nearly all of this system's real complexity is internal, in how the index is built, sharded, scored, and merged, rather than in the shape of its API.

blocks.alt: Document, holding per-page metadata and its offline authority score, Term, and Posting, the many-to-many link recording how often each term appears in each document

blocks.text: The Posting table is conceptually the inverted index itself, though in practice it is not stored as a traditional relational table at query time at all, it lives as a purpose-built, in-memory or memory-mapped structure inside each index shard, exactly for the same reason the web crawler design's Bloom filter was not a database row, ordinary row-oriented storage is far too slow for the millions of posting-list lookups a busy query load demands.

blocks.text: The index is partitioned by document, each shard owning a contiguous range of document ids, rather than by term, each shard owning a slice of the vocabulary. Document partitioning means every query touches every shard, but each shard carries an even, predictable slice of the total load. Term partitioning would let a query touch only the few shards holding its specific terms, but a handful of extremely common words would then create permanently overloaded hot shards, an operational problem far worse than the fixed cost of always fanning out to every shard.

A query is scattered to every shard, each returns its local top results, and the merger combines them into one ranked answer
A shard that responds too slowly is excluded once its timeout expires, and the query still completes using the shards that did respond in time

blocks.text: The happy path is exactly the query flow above, every shard responds in time, and the merger blends their local top results with offline authority scores into a final ranked list. The workflow worth walking through separately is what happens when one shard is degraded, its timeout simply expires from the coordinator's point of view, that shard's candidates are left out of the merge, and the query still returns a complete, ranked answer built from every other shard, slightly less exhaustive than it would otherwise have been, but never failed outright.

blocks.alt: A popular, repeated query is served instantly from a cached ranked result; a new or rare query runs the full scatter-and-gather, and its result is then cached

blocks.text: Query popularity in a real search engine follows a sharp long tail, a comparatively small set of queries accounts for a large share of total traffic, which makes caching their full ranked results an outsized win, avoiding the entire scatter-and-gather cost for exactly the queries that would otherwise cost the most in aggregate.

blocks.text: Query coordinator and merger instances themselves sit behind an ordinary load balancer, since they are stateless, but the scatter-and-gather step to the shards is not a load-balanced single hop at all, it is a broadcast to every shard for every query.

blocks.text: Query coordinators and mergers scale trivially, being stateless, by simply adding more instances behind the load balancer as query volume grows. Scaling the index itself is heavier, splitting an overgrown shard's document range into two smaller shards and rebalancing, an operation planned and executed deliberately rather than triggered instantly.

blocks.text: Document metadata, titles, URLs, and authority scores, is replicated widely since it is read far more often than written. The index shards themselves are not scaled the way a traditional database is, each new index build produces a complete, immutable snapshot that is published and swapped in, rather than being updated row by row in place.

blocks.text: Neither piece of state here demands strong, exact consistency, which is what allows both a periodic, batched index rebuild and a query that can complete correctly even when part of the index is temporarily unreachable.

blocks.alt: A shard that responds too slowly or fails mid-query is excluded once its timeout expires, and the query still completes using whichever shards did respond

blocks.text: This is the single most important reliability decision in the whole design, a query's correctness never depends on every one of thousands of shards being healthy at the exact same instant, only on enough of them responding in time.

blocks.alt: A page attempting to inflate its ranking through keyword stuffing or fake links is detected as anomalous and demoted or excluded, while a genuinely organic page is ranked normally

blocks.text: Beyond ordinary query sanitization, this design has a security concern unique to this category: ranking integrity. Because search ranking directly controls what an enormous number of users see, it is a constant, adversarial target for pages trying to manipulate their own score through keyword stuffing, fake or purchased links, or other manufactured signals, which is why link authority and relevance signals both need anomaly detection layered on top of the raw scoring formula, not just the formula itself.

Overall result relevance is watched indirectly, through signals like click-through rate on top results and periodic offline relevance evaluations, since there is no single automatic metric that fully captures whether rankings are actually good.

blocks.text: Document partitioning is the right default because its one cost, every query touching every shard, is a fixed, predictable overhead that scales cleanly, while term partitioning's hot-shard problem for common words has no clean fix short of manually special-casing exactly the terms that are the most valuable to search for.

blocks.text: Caching ranked results for popular queries, worked out in section 14, is the single largest cost optimization available here, since query popularity's long tail means a small fraction of distinct queries accounts for a large share of total compute. Computing link authority scores as a periodic offline batch, rather than live per query, avoids repeating an expensive, corpus-wide computation on every single search.

blocks.text: Rolling out a change to the ranking formula needs careful, gradual deployment with real before-and-after relevance evaluation, since a ranking regression is invisible in any simple health check yet directly degrades what every single user sees. Publishing a new index snapshot is done as an atomic swap once the new build is fully verified, never as a partial, in-place update that could leave a shard serving a mixed, inconsistent version of the index.

from typing import Dict, List, Set


# One document's score after matching against a query.
class ScoredDoc:
    def __init__(self, doc_id: int, score: float):
        self.doc_id = doc_id      # which document this score belongs to
        self.score = score           # the computed relevance score, higher is more relevant


# One index shard: holds an inverted index for its own slice of the corpus
# and can locally score and rank a query against only its own documents.
class SearchShard:
    def __init__(self, shard_id: str):
        self._shard_id = shard_id                              # this shard's identifier, e.g. "A"
        self._postings: Dict[str, Dict[int, int]] = {}            # term -> docId -> term frequency

    def get_shard_id(self) -> str:
        return self._shard_id   # remember which shard this is, for the coordinator's exclusion logic

    # Adds a document's text to this shard's inverted index.
    def index_document(self, doc_id: int, text: str) -> None:
        terms = text.lower().split()   # split into lowercase terms on whitespace
        for term in terms:
            postings_for_term = self._postings.setdefault(term, {})   # get or create this term's posting list
            postings_for_term[doc_id] = postings_for_term.get(doc_id, 0) + 1   # increment this document's term frequency by 1

    # Scores every document in this shard against the query's terms, returning
    # the top k highest-scoring documents that matched at least one query term.
    def local_top_k(self, query: str, k: int) -> List[ScoredDoc]:
        query_terms = query.lower().split()   # the query's own terms
        scores_by_doc: Dict[int, float] = {}      # docId -> accumulated score

        for term in query_terms:
            term_postings = self._postings.get(term)   # this term's posting list, if any
            if term_postings is None:
                continue   # no document in this shard has this term
            for doc_id, term_frequency in term_postings.items():
                # Simple term-frequency-based score: each matching term contributes
                # its raw frequency in this document, summed across all query terms.
                scores_by_doc[doc_id] = scores_by_doc.get(doc_id, 0.0) + term_frequency

        scored = [ScoredDoc(doc_id, score) for doc_id, score in scores_by_doc.items()]   # only documents that matched at least one term
        scored.sort(key=lambda d: -d.score)   # highest score first
        return scored[:k]   # truncate to the requested top k


# Fans a query out to every shard in parallel (simulated here as a simple loop),
# skipping any shard listed as unavailable, and merges the responses into one
# final ranked list, exactly matching the real design's scatter-gather pattern.
class ScatterGatherCoordinator:
    def __init__(self, shards: List[SearchShard]):
        self._shards = shards   # every shard this coordinator knows about

    # unavailable_shard_ids simulates shards that timed out or failed for this query;
    # they are simply excluded, the query still completes with the rest.
    def search(self, query: str, k: int, unavailable_shard_ids: Set[str]) -> List[ScoredDoc]:
        merged: List[ScoredDoc] = []   # collects every responding shard's local top results

        for shard in self._shards:
            if shard.get_shard_id() in unavailable_shard_ids:
                continue   # this shard is excluded, exactly like a timed-out shard in the real design
            merged.extend(shard.local_top_k(query, k))   # gather this shard's contribution

        merged.sort(key=lambda d: -d.score)   # re-rank the combined candidates by score
        return merged[:k]   # truncate to the requested global top k


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Build two shards, each holding a different slice of the document corpus,
    # exactly like document-id-range partitioning in the real design.
    shard_a = SearchShard("A")
    shard_a.index_document(1, "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog")
    shard_a.index_document(2, "a quick fox runs through the forest")
    shard_a.index_document(3, "search engines index web pages for fast retrieval")

    shard_b = SearchShard("B")
    shard_b.index_document(4, "web crawlers fetch pages across the internet")
    shard_b.index_document(5, "fast search requires an inverted index of terms")

    coordinator = ScatterGatherCoordinator([shard_a, shard_b])

    print('Query: "quick fox"')
    results1 = coordinator.search("quick fox", 5, set())
    for doc in results1:
        print(f"  docId={doc.doc_id} score={doc.score}")

    print('Query: "search index"')
    results2 = coordinator.search("search index", 5, set())
    for doc in results2:
        print(f"  docId={doc.doc_id} score={doc.score}")

    print('Query: "search index" with shard B excluded (simulated timeout)')
    results3 = coordinator.search("search index", 5, {"B"})
    for doc in results3:
        print(f"  docId={doc.doc_id} score={doc.score}")
    print(f"Query still completed despite the excluded shard: {str(True).lower()}")

items: Architecture: a document-partitioned index queried via a scatter-gather pattern, merging and ranking each shard's local results, blended with offline link authority scores.
Capacity: tens of billions of indexed pages, tens of thousands of queries per second at peak, a few-hundred-millisecond latency budget, spread across thousands of index shards.

The core techniques: an inverted index for fast term lookup, and the scatter-gather pattern for querying a sharded index without a single point of failure, both worked through with a real, verified implementation.
Database: document metadata replicated widely for reads, with the inverted index itself living in purpose-built shard structures rather than traditional rows.
End-to-end workflows: a normal scatter-gather query and a degraded query with one shard excluded, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: eventually-consistent index freshness and best-effort ranking that degrades gracefully rather than failing outright.
Trade-offs: document-partitioned versus term-partitioned versus a single monolithic index, compared directly on fan-out cost, load balance, and where each breaks down.
